reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive deficiency of the inner-membrane enzyme that regenerates long-chain acyl-CoA from acylcarnitine after it has crossed into the mitochondrion
Three phenotypes: a lethal neonatal form with malformations, a severe infantile hepatocardiomuscular form, and a common milder adult myopathic form

The adult myopathic form (the commonest) presents with recurrent exercise-induced or fasting-induced rhabdomyolysis and myoglobinuria, often triggered by prolonged exertion, cold or intercurrent illness
The c.338C>T (p.Ser113Leu) variant is the most frequent mutation in the myopathic phenotype
Acylcarnitine profile shows raised long-chain species, particularly palmitoylcarnitine (C16) and oleoylcarnitine/stearoylcarnitine (C18:1, C18), with a high (C16+C18:1)/C2 ratio
Between attacks, muscle strength and creatine kinase are typically normal in the myopathic form
Management involves avoidance of fasting and prolonged exercise, high-carbohydrate cover around exertion, and long-chain fat restriction with medium-chain triglyceride in more severe phenotypes
reference.pathophysiology: Carnitine palmitoyltransferase 2 is located on the inner face of the inner mitochondrial membrane and reconverts long-chain acylcarnitines, delivered by the translocase, back to acyl-CoA esters for beta-oxidation within the matrix. When the enzyme is deficient, long-chain fatty acids cannot be oxidised despite entering the mitochondrion, so tissues dependent on fatty-acid energy fail during fasting, exertion or catabolic stress. In the myopathic form, energy shortfall and accumulation of long-chain acylcarnitines during sustained exercise damage muscle fibres, causing rhabdomyolysis; severe neonatal and infantile forms reflect near-complete loss of activity with multi-organ involvement.
additionalDifferentials: McArdle disease and other metabolic myopathies with exertional intolerance
Other causes of recurrent rhabdomyolysis (drugs, toxins, dystrophinopathies)
Neonatal cardiomyopathy or dysmorphism of other metabolic cause
additionalInvestigations: Plasma acylcarnitine profile showing elevated C16 and C18:1 long-chain acylcarnitines
Creatine kinase and urinary myoglobin during exertional or fasting episodes
Blood glucose, ketones, ammonia and lactate during acute illness in severe forms
Echocardiography and ECG in infantile/neonatal presentations
CPT2 molecular genetic testing including the common p.Ser113Leu variant
Fibroblast or muscle enzyme assay where genotype is inconclusive
redFlags: Pigmenturia with markedly raised creatine kinase and risk of acute kidney injury
Cardiac arrhythmia or cardiomyopathy in infantile/neonatal forms
Hypoketotic hypoglycaemia with encephalopathy in severe phenotypes
Rapidly progressive multi-organ failure in the neonatal lethal form
reference.prognosis: The adult myopathic form is compatible with a normal lifespan when rhabdomyolysis triggers are avoided, whereas the infantile and neonatal forms carry high morbidity and mortality despite treatment.
pitfalls: Missing the diagnosis in an adult with recurrent exertional muscle pain and normal interictal examination
Failing to provide carbohydrate cover before prolonged or strenuous exercise
Not monitoring renal function during severe rhabdomyolysis
Assuming a normal creatine kinase between attacks excludes the disorder
references: Scriver's OMMBID (Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease)
management: Avoid triggers of rhabdomyolysis, including prolonged exercise, fasting, cold exposure and intercurrent illness
Dietary restriction of long-chain fat with a high-carbohydrate intake supplemented by medium-chain triglycerides, ensuring carbohydrate before and during exertion
Emergency regimen during illness or catabolic stress with intravenous glucose to suppress lipolysis and prevent metabolic decompensation
Acute management of rhabdomyolysis with generous intravenous fluids and monitoring to prevent myoglobinuric acute kidney injury
Cardiac assessment with echocardiography and electrocardiography plus multi-organ support in the infantile and neonatal forms
Metabolic specialist and dietitian follow-up with a written emergency plan
Genetic counselling and family screening for this autosomal recessive disorder, including the common p.Ser113Leu variant
